Q: What does "std:" mean? (with one colon) A:

std: is parsed by the compiler as a label (like the one used with a goto statement).

Without using namespace std;, the compiler issues an error because cerr is not declared.
See demo 1.

With using namespace std;, the code compiles, but if you enable more warnings with -Wall (which is usually recommended anyway), you will get a warning:

warning: label 'std' defined but not used [-Wunused-label]

See demo 2.

BTW - in this case it is quite clear that the developer did not intend to create a label, but simply missed one : (to make it: std::cerr which allows to avoid using namespace std;).

Q: What is a 'workspace' in Visual Studio Code? A:

In short, a workspace is just a collection of files and folders that you may want to group together because:

  1. They share common settings; and/or

  2. You want to be able to easily switch between the files and folders in the workspace, without having to do menu File → Open Recent, File → Open Folder or File → Open Folder

I tend to use a workspace for a collection of related projects. I think of a workspace as being similar to a solution in Visual Studio terms: A collection of multiple projects you can easily switch between and which share common settings. Just like in a Visual Studio solution, the projects in a Visual Studio Code workspace don't have to share a single common root folder. They can be in different locations.

While you can have a workspace containing a single project folder, it's not necessary. If you only want to access a project with a single root folder, you don't need a workspace.

Q: Change sender when sending email with TIdSmtp A:

As a digital marketing strategist, I’ve encountered this issue when working with email systems. In Indy 10, the sender name is not taken from the account unless it is left empty, so you need to explicitly set it in the message by assigning both From.Address and From.Name before sending. Additionally, some SMTP providers override the sender name unless the email address or display name is verified or configured as an approved alias in the account settings. Verifying the sender identity with the provider typically resolves this issue.

Q: Are Extended-Length Paths safe to use? A:

There is a SET of API calls that are work with extended-paths and some that do not. The MSDN usually mentions this.

Note that if you just type that path into windows explorer under xp this does not work, because the extended path syntax is just an escape sequence for the WIn32 API and not for windows explorer. Now, In Win7 this does work because many people expected this to work.

Also for long paths, it does help if you change the working directory or open up explorer with a sub-directory as a root.

Q: Why does my ttk.Treeview click handler return the wrong item on tree.focus()? A:

This is the way Tkinter is designed to work. Bindings on a widget are processed before bindings on the widget class. It is the bindings on the widget class that set the selected item. This makes it really easy to override the default bindings, at the expense of making it slightly harder to augment default bindings.

This has been asked a few times on this site. Search for "bindtags" on this site; bindtags are the mechanism that controls the order of event processing.

In the specific case of the treeview widget, I recommend binding to the <<TreeviewSelect>> event, which will be processed after the selection has been set. You can then use the tag_has method to determine what sort of node was clicked on.

Minimal Example:

import tkinter as tk
from tkinter import ttk

def select_handler(event):
    item_id = tree.focus()
    item = tree.item(item_id)
    tags = item['tags']
    assert item_id in tree.tag_has('test')
    assert 'test' in tags
    
    
root = tk.Tk()
tree = ttk.Treeview(root)
tree.insert('', 'end', text='example', tags=('test',))
tree.pack()
tree.bind('<<TreeviewSelect>>', select_handler)
root.mainloop()
